facts.text: Measles is caused by a highly contagious virus that spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes.
The measles virus can stay active in the air or on surfaces for up to two hours.
One person with measles can infect up to 18 other people.
Measles usually begins with fever, runny nose, cough and red eyes; a rash follows a few days later, starting on the face and spreading down the body.
Unvaccinated young children face the highest risk of severe measles.
The measles vaccine has been used since 1963; it is safe and effective and costs less than one US dollar per child.
WHO recommends two doses of measles vaccine; in high-risk countries the first dose is usually given at nine months of age.
Measles vaccination prevented an estimated 59 million deaths between 2000 and 2024.
WHO and UNICEF said the drop in childhood vaccination seen in 2021 was the largest sustained decline in about 30 years, driven by COVID-19 disruptions.
Childhood immunization began to recover in 2022.
The World Bank indicator counts children aged 12 to 23 months who had received a measles vaccine (at least one dose).
